our_rationale: The eastern feature is a thin (~0.2") blue arc holding radius ~1.5" from PA 40 to 140 with its centre of curvature within ~0.15" of the ticked nucleus, and a blue compact knot sits at r~1.0", PA 270, directly opposite its midpoint - a classic two-image/partial-ring configuration seen in the direct panels (a,b,c,d,e), not only in the subtracted residual.

Items 1 and 2 survive: in panels (a), (b), (d), (e) and again as an offset ridge in the subtracted panel (f) there is a thin (~0.15-0.2" FWHM) ridge sweeping from due east through south to the southwest of the ticked nucleus at r~1.1-1.5" over ~110-130 deg of azimuth, concave toward the deflector, detached from the bulge across a low-surface-brightness gap, with a thickened tan-coloured knot south-southeast in (e) against the white-cored deflector; width/radius ~0.12-0.15 is far thinner than any host resonance ring or shell, the radius does not grow with angle so it is not a spiral arm, no diffraction spikes or striping exist in the field, and the big SW spiral at r~4-4.7" lies on the convex side so the ridge does not curve about it. Both critics independently and correctly removed item 3: the NNW patch is where the host's own isophotes already run, it is smooth, coreless and shares the halo hue, and the large NW blob in (f) is the circular-model core mis-subtraction at only ~0.6". What is left is a compelling one-sided tangential arc with no counter-image, and geometry's circle fit through the arc in (d) puts its curvature centre ~1" NW of the ticked nucleus with R~2.2" rather than concentric with it - consistent either with a lens whose mass centroid is offset/elliptical or with an interaction feature involving the nearby SW spiral. That residual tension, not a hedge, is why a human or a lens model with the counter-image prediction tested would settle it; on the evidence in front of me this is a probable lens.

The dominant feature is the bright, thin streak lying ~2.3-2.8" west-northwest of the ticked elliptical: in the normal 10" panel it is a sharp crescent whose concave edge faces the core, in the deep panel it keeps its narrow, roughly constant width against a radius many times larger, and in the two-band colour panel it is distinctly orange against the whiter deflector light - a plausible dusty background source. It is present in every un-subtracted panel, so it is not a subtraction product, and its only appearance in the zooms is where its outer tip clips the top-right corner of (d), (e), (f); the four-lobed bowtie dominating (f) is the expected circular-model artefact and was correctly ignored. Two critics argued for an edge-on disc, but the pixels do not show a straight ridge with a central bulge and pointed tips; the streak bends, and its centre of curvature lies close to the deflector nucleus, which is the signature of a tangential arc. What keeps this from an A is the missing counter-image: the E/SE side at comparable radius shows only isotropic mottling (item 3, correctly killed by the artifact critic), and the saturated halo plus the circular-model residual make a clean search there impossible in this rendering. A reviewer with a proper elliptical-model subtraction, or deeper multiband data to test the streak for an internal disc profile versus a lensed source spectrum, would settle whether this is a fold arc or a fortuitously placed inclined disc, so B (probable) with human follow-up.

Both items survive: in panels (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) a thin crescent runs from about PA 100 to PA 170 at r = 1.30-1.50" southeast of the ticked nucleus, concave toward that nucleus, with its long axis at the local tangent to within ~10 deg, and it reappears in (f) as an offset tangential feature far outside the r<0.8" dipole/bowtie wedges that the 1-D circular model necessarily produces on this obviously elliptical galaxy - so it is not a subtraction artefact, and its smooth curvature at fixed radius excludes spikes, striping, seams or PSF wings (artifact and geometry critics both declined to offer an alternative). The morphology critic's shell/stream reading is overruled on the pixels: the feature is ~1/8 of its radius in width, colour-distinct from the orange envelope, shows no stellar bridge to the nucleus and no monotonic radius growth, and carries a brightness maximum along its southern half consistent with a fold, whereas a shell would be broad, host-coloured and profile-matched. The one shortfall is the counter-image: the NW quadrant at r = 1.2-1.9", PA 280-350 is swamped by the bright envelope in every direct panel and by the circular-model artefact in (f), so it is uninformative rather than negative, which holds this at probable (B) rather than A.

What survives is the feature that matters: in the 3.5" deep zoom (d) and again, sharply, in the subtracted panel (f), a chain of three-to-four compact knots runs from about (r=1.45", PA 93) to (r=1.27", PA 141) on the east/south-east side of the ticked galaxy, concave toward it, with a fainter low-surface-brightness continuation curving on under the core toward the south at essentially the same radius - roughly 100° of tangential extent about a centre of curvature within ~0.3" of the nucleus. It is present in the un-subtracted panels (a), (b), (d) and (e), so it is not a subtraction residual, and it lies far outside the r<0.6" butterfly/ring pattern the circular profile leaves in (f); the artifact critic found no spike, snowball, striping or PSF wing touching it, and the geometry critic could not break its tangentiality. The morphology critic's tidal-envelope reading is overruled because the diffuse light it invokes belongs to the big extended galaxy occupying the SE corner of the 10" panels at r>4" and never turns tangential under the deflector core the way the (f) feature does. What is genuinely lost is the counter-image: the NW point at r≈1.9", PA≈301 is antipodal in angle but 40% too far out and morphologically round, so it is as easily a projected companion in this crowded group as a fourth image - which is exactly why this reads as a probable rather than a certain lens, and why deeper or multi-band data (or a human reviewer weighing the tidal environment) would settle it.

Both critics who named an alternative attacked only item 4, and the pixels back them: the western object visible in (b), (d) and (e) is round and PSF-like with no tangential stretch, so it is a companion projection and drops out. Nothing was offered against items 1-3, and the artifact critic explicitly cleared the field (no spikes on the core, no striping, no snowball, and every item traceable in un-subtracted panels a/b/d/e, so subtraction_residual is inadmissible). What survives is the southern feature: in (a) and (b) a thin curved ridge sitting ~1.3-1.45" south of the ticked nucleus, sweeping ~80 deg of azimuth at essentially constant radius with its centre of curvature within ~0.25-0.3" of the core, concave toward it, and thickness only ~1/5 of its radius - too thin and too radius-constant for a spiral arm (no radial growth with angle, no stellar bridge from the nucleus) and not a closed host ring or shell (no north-side counterpart at r~1.35" in the deep panels). The embedded brighter knot at its west/SW end (item 2) and the compact blue-white blob at r~0.85" due south (item 3), bluer than the yellow-white envelope in (c)/(e), reinforce a lensed-source reading, and the same crescent reappears as an offset, non-mirrored feature in (f) rather than as the butterfly/ring pattern the circular model would produce. Against a grade A stands the absence of any separable counter-arc north of the core inside the saturated halo, and the possibility that the bright southern blob is itself a companion whose own mass shapes the arc; that ambiguity is real and would be settled by a reviewer with deeper or higher-resolution multi-band data, hence B and needs_human.

The evidence is the thin orange filament that sweeps over the north side of the ticked elliptical in (a), (b) and (c): it is ~0.3-0.4" thick against a 2.0-3.5" standoff (width/radius ~0.12), concave toward the galaxy through ~150 deg of azimuth, separated from the host's outermost isophotes by a dark gap at r~1.2-1.6" in (d) with no stellar bridge, and distinctly orange in (c)/(e) where the host core is white-yellow and the SE companion is bluish. The artifact critic correctly shows the only instrumental signature is the near-vertical 1/f striping that cuts straight across the curved band without following it, and the morphology critic correctly finds a clean, featureless ellipsoid in (d) with no arms, bar, knots, double nucleus or host-profiled shell that could produce it; the bright band along the top of (f) is traceable in the un-subtracted (d)/(e), so it is not one of the circular-model bowtie lobes (those are the two large symmetric N/S wedges plus the central dipole speckle). What holds the grade below A is the geometry critic's real measurement: the filament's radius from the deflector varies by ~60-70% along its length and its curvature radius (~4-5") exceeds its standoff, so it is not a clean fixed-radius Einstein arc, and the only counter-image candidate (item 3, the SSW diffuse fan at r~1.3", PA 190-240) sits at half the arc radius, is halo-like rather than filamentary, and overlaps the southern model lobe - it cannot be used as confirmation. A tidal streamer/plume associated with the compact SE neighbour ~3.5" away therefore remains open, but it is not favoured by the arc's thinness, its colour offset from the host, or the absent bridge. Deeper multi-band imaging or a reviewer's eye on the arc's surface-brightness profile and on the SSW patch would settle whether this is a wide-separation group-assisted arc or a stream.

What survives is a single feature: the thin, bright, continuously curved band on the eastern flank of the ticked galaxy at r~1", running roughly PA 15 through 90 to 160, clearly visible in the un-subtracted deep zoom (d) and as an orange/tan band in colour zoom (e), and reappearing in (f) as a one-sided offset ridge at near-constant radius rather than as one of the butterfly lobes or concentric rings the circular-profile subtraction would produce - the artefact critic's checks (no 6-spike pattern, no seam or stripe, band present in every direct panel) leave it untouched. Against it: the putative counter-image at PA~280 is plainly a separate small galaxy with its own compact nucleus, elongated radially toward the deflector at 1.6x the arc radius, so the system has no confirmed counter-image; and the southern clump chain at r~2.2-2.7" plus the SSE flare are naturally read as a star-forming outer arm embedded in the same brown, dusty envelope that fills the 10" colour panel, with a matching faint filament on the NW side. The arc's width (~0.2" at the eastern segment, well under its radius) and its centre of curvature within ~0.3-0.4" of the nucleus keep a lens interpretation alive, but an inner dust-lane-bounded spiral arm of a mildly inclined disc reproduces the same pixels, and with the counter-image removed nothing breaks the tie. C, and a reviewer or resolved colour/spectroscopy of the eastern band would settle it.

Two of the scorer's three items fall: the eastern knots (item 2) are independently shown by both the geometry and morphology critics to be a chain of discrete compact blobs stepping outward from r~1.6" to ~3.5" along PA 60-105 in the deep 10" panel, round rather than tangentially stretched, with no counterpart on the west side of any direct panel - a projected clumpy neighbour, not a tangential image; and the west patch (item 3) exists only in panel (f) at the margin of the core's vertical ringing, with the corresponding pixels in (d) and (e) perfectly smooth, so it is a property of the 1-D circular fit (helped by the unmodelled wing gradient of the bright galaxy ~4" west) and is inadmissible as evidence. What survives is item 1: the thin low-surface-brightness wisp sweeping from ESE round to south at r~1.5", concave toward the ticked galaxy, which is visible in the un-subtracted panels (a) and (b) and reappears in (f) as an offset curved ridge along the southern edge at roughly constant radius rather than as a core-symmetric ring. One curved, direct-panel-confirmed feature with a plausible centre of curvature (~0.4" offset) but no confirmed counter-image and no colour contrast strong enough to help in a two-band render leaves the case genuinely open; the same arc could be a tidal shell or an outer stellar-envelope feature of this smooth spheroid. That is a textbook C, and a reviewer with a deeper or elliptical-model subtraction that follows the southern ridge through 100-175 deg and searches the north-west for its counterpart would settle it.

Both critics converge on the same target and both are upheld: the bright, round, unresolved-core blob 0.9" WSW of the tick centre in panels (d), (e) and (f) shows no tangential elongation and no counterpart at PA~74, so item 4 is a companion/satellite projection and is removed. What survives are items 1-3, the filamentary structures seen plainly in the un-subtracted 10" panels (a) and (b): a knotty streak arching over the top of the halo from the NE quadrant to the NW at r~1.9-2.3", concave toward the core, plus fainter segments to the E (~2.6") and W/SW (~2.8"). The artifact critic correctly finds no spike, seam or striping explanation - these are curved, at roughly fixed radius, and absent from any straight-edge pattern - and the morphology critic finds no stellar bridge from the nucleus and no smooth radius-vs-angle growth inside 1.75", where the host is featureless. But the evidence stops short of confirming a lens: the segment radii spread by a factor ~1.5, the northern feature is knotty rather than a smooth thin band and in (b) it merges with further wisps that trail outward toward the NE corner of the 10" field, which is exactly what a shell/tidal or outer-arm system around a big halo produces; the two-band colour in (c) shows the northern streak neutral-to-tan, not distinctly offset from the host, and the inner 1.7" is saturated in the direct zoom so no inner counter-image can be tested. Panel (f)'s central radiating streaks and lobes are the expected circular-profile residual and carry no weight. This sits genuinely between a broken Einstein ring and a shell/arm system: deeper multi-band imaging or a proper elliptical-model subtraction would settle whether the northern knots share a colour and surface-brightness profile with the E and W segments, so a human reviewer is warranted.

What survives is a single feature: the thin bright ridge on the western (right-hand) side of panels (a)/(b), which in the circular-subtracted 10" panel (c) stands out as an offset, coreless, knotty filament curving concave toward the ticks at roughly constant radius r~4.0-5.0" over PA~250-315 - it is not the central bowtie/ripple artefact, it is traceable in both un-subtracted 10" panels, and it holds no fixed position angle so it is neither a spike nor a frame edge (the artifact critic found no reduction-artefact match and named no alternative). Everything else that made the case for lensing has fallen: the r=1.3" ENE source in the 3.5" zoom is a stellar, nucleus-like peak sharing a continuous envelope with the ticked galaxy and has no counterpart at PA~249, and the SE object at r~4.6" is a resolved galaxy with its own bright core and a plume whose major axis is ~45 deg from the local tangent - so the putative counter-image and inner knot are a close pair and a group member, not multiple images. That leaves one arc-like feature with no counter-arc, on a deflector that is itself an interacting pair whose asymmetric tidal envelope reaches out to roughly that radius; the ridge's thinness and near-constant radius keep lensing alive, but a tidal shell/plume edge is equally consistent with these pixels in a single band with no colour to compare stellar populations. That is a genuine ambiguity that deeper or multi-band imaging (or a reviewer tracing the ridge's surface-brightness profile against the host's) would settle, hence C and needs_human.

What survives is the orange, tangentially elongated pair in panel (c): a curved streak running over the N/NW flank at r~3.0-3.3" (PA~295-355), concave toward the ticked core, and a second orange segment of the same hue and comparable surface brightness on the SE/S side at r~3.0" (PA~105-160), roughly opposite across the white deflector whose core is distinctly bluer in the two-band colour. Both are present in the un-subtracted panels (a), (b) and (c), so the artifact critic is right that the panel-(f) hourglass and concentric ripples - the documented circular-profile artefact on an elliptical host - explain nothing here, and no spike, stripe or PSF wing from the bright SW streak reaches PA 295-355. The spiral-arm reading fails on the pixels: the 3.5" zoom (d,e) is a featureless smooth spheroid with no inner arm continuation, and the residual bowtie is the signature of an ellipsoid, not a disc. What keeps this from being a B is the environment visible in the deep 10" stretch: broad diffuse plumes wrap the whole envelope, a blue interloper sits at the NE corner, a bright elongated object cuts the SW corner, and the compact knot at PA~180, r~2.7" carries its own tail toward that object - a tidal/shell or projected-debris origin for the same orange loops cannot be excluded at this depth, and the SE segment is patchy where a counter-arc should be smooth and matched in profile. Deeper or multi-band imaging (or a proper elliptical-model subtraction to test whether the two orange segments share a source colour and lie on a common curvature centre) would settle it.

The ticked object is not a relaxed deflector: panels (d) and (e) resolve two nuclei ~1.1" apart inside a single boxy envelope that bulges SW, and the 10" panels show further companions NE and SE, so any interpretation must contend with an ongoing merger in a group-scale envelope. Items 2 and 3 fall to that context - the brightenings on the western edge are resolved compact sources with their own haloes (a near-identical one sits at r~4.3", PA~158 on the east side), and the SW patch is one of them, so the knot-chain argument does not carry weight. What survives is item 1: in panels (a), (b) and (c) alike there is a thin, sharp, coherently curved filament along the western field edge running from roughly PA 225 to PA 310 at r~3.6-4.5", concave toward the pair, present in the un-subtracted deep stretch and therefore not a product of the circular 1-D subtraction. That is genuinely arc-like, but it is equally the classic appearance of a shell/plume flung along the merger axis defined by the secondary nucleus at PA~248, and it is thin, low-contrast and offers no confirmed counter-image: item 4 (r~2.6", PA~97) appears only in the deflector-subtracted 10" residual, exactly where the azimuthally-averaged model leaves lobes and a dipole on this off-centre, companion-blended galaxy, so it cannot be counted either way. With one real tangential feature, no counter-image in any direct panel, and a merger that supplies a competing origin, the evidence neither confirms nor refutes lensing; colour or deeper multi-band imaging (matching profiles between the western filament and any eastern counterpart) would settle it, which is why a human reviewer is warranted.

What survives is a single feature: the thin, one-sided sliver about 1.0" ESE of the tick centre in the deflector-subtracted zoom (f), concave toward the nucleus, brighter than the surrounding ~0.15"-spaced profile ripples, and matching a faint halo asymmetry on the same side in (d)/(e). Everything else is explained away: the fainter r~1.5" clump is indistinguishable from the ringing that fills (f) (it appears in no direct panel), and the broad diffuse light at PA 60-120 is plainly the one-sided bridge to the disturbed companion 2.7" east in (a)/(b)/(c), part of a chain of interacting group members with plumes to the NE - not a halo centred on the deflector. The surviving sliver is not enough for a lens: there is no counter-image anywhere at r~0.9-1.5", PA 275-315 in (d) or (e) (the halo there looks smooth at this stretch), its curvature centre is offset ~0.25-0.3" east of the nucleus, and it sits on the same side as, and roughly along, the tidal axis toward the companion, so tidal debris remains a live competitor for it. The tangential curvature and the fact that it exceeds the local ripple amplitude keep a lensed arc formally possible, hence C rather than D. A reviewer with a proper elliptical (or PSF-convolved Sersic) subtraction, or any third band, could decide immediately whether that sliver is a stream fragment or the visible half of an Einstein arc, so this is a genuine ambiguity worth human time.

The only real evidence is the LW-bright (orange) material ~1.1-1.5" N/NNE of the ticked nucleus: it is obvious in the colour zoom (e) and the 10" colour panel (c), reappears as a bright offset irregular patch in the subtracted panel (f) well away from the central dipole/butterfly of the circular-profile model, and is faintly traceable in the deep panels (b)/(d). Against a lens: the patch is chunky rather than a thin fixed-radius arc (its width is comparable to its ~1.2" radius in (f)), its outer edge merges into a spur that continues radially outward to r~2.3" in the 10" deep frame, and there is no counter-image - the S/SSW 'item 2' is only a smooth isophote bulge in (d) plus streaking-level noise in (b), which the artifact critic's upheld striping call removes entirely. Against a clean rejection: the two critics who both invoked companion_projection disagree by ~50 deg on the feature's own position angle (21 deg off tangential vs within 10 deg of radial), and the orange material in (c)/(e) does extend across the top of the core to the NNW rather than sitting as a single wedge, so a short tangential segment at PA~330-10 is not accounted for. Item 1 therefore survives in reduced form as an unresolved arc-versus-superposed-neighbour ambiguity: possible, not confirmed, and a reviewer with the pixel data (or an extra band / redshift for the NNE clump) could settle whether the NNE patch and the NNW band are one fixed-radius structure or a projected companion plus halo colour gradient.

The catalogued galaxy at the yellow ticks is a smooth, saturated envelope - panels (d) and (e) show a monotonic, featureless halo out to 1.75" with no inner arc, ring or knot, and the checkerboard/butterfly in (f) is the expected circular-profile artefact and carries no weight. Everything rests on two thin low-surface-brightness streaks straddling the nucleus at r~2-3" in the 10" panels: the eastern one (left of the core, ~40-70 px east and a little south in (a)/(b), also faintly orange in (c)) and a comparable western one (right of the core in (a)/(b)). Both geometry and morphology critics independently measured the eastern feature's long axis at PA~130-135, i.e. within ~30 deg of the radius vector and ~60 deg from tangential, and it is compact and needle-like rather than curving about the tick centre; that upholds a projected edge-on/companion interloper and removes item 1. Item 2, the western streak, is left standing by both critics and is the only surviving evidence, but it too is elongated close to the radial direction and lies almost on the same line through the nucleus as item 1, which is at least as consistent with a single superposed needle or a tidal plume as with a counter-image; with no tangential curvature, no third image and nothing inside 1.75", the evidence neither confirms nor refutes lensing, hence C. A reviewer with the full-resolution frame (or any second-epoch/multi-band data) could decide whether the two opposite streaks are one edge-on disc seen through the envelope, which would settle this to D.

What survives is a single feature: in the 10" deep panel (b) a thin low-surface-brightness filament wraps the south/south-east flank of the ticked galaxy from PA~110 round to ~215 at r~1.2-1.5", concave toward the core, and the same flux reappears in the subtracted zoom (f) as a one-sided bright fan/wedge SE-S of the nucleus with nothing mirrored to the north - a one-sided offset feature, not the four-lobed butterfly or concentric ring the circular profile subtraction manufactures, so it is admissible and is also traceable in the un-subtracted (b)/(d). Against it: the feature is broad and merges into the halo rather than showing a thin, structured arc, the deep zoom (d) is saturated inside ~0.8" so no inner counter-image can be checked, the artifact critic correctly finds no diffraction ray, striping (columnar N-S) or neighbour halo (r~3.6", PA~121) that can make a constant-radius 105-deg feature, and the only candidate second image - the NE blob at r~1.7", PA~44 - is round, at a ~25% discrepant radius, and is upheld as a projection, leaving the arc with no counter-image family. The sharp outer edge and the clumpy envelope in (c) keep a tidal-shell or outer-disc origin genuinely open, so the evidence neither confirms nor refutes lensing; a reviewer with a proper elliptical-model subtraction or multi-band colour on the SE filament would settle it.

The catalogued galaxy at the yellow ticks resolves in the 3.5" deep and normal zooms into a lumpy, irregular envelope: three to four compact peaks inside r<0.4" (NE at PA~45, W/SW at PA~250, an E/SE chain at r~0.30-0.38"), every one of them round to within the PSF with no measurable tangential elongation, none of them lying on a common circle about the tick centre, and all of them connected to the nucleus by continuous emission that never drops to background between knot and core. The residual panel (f) reproduces exactly these peaks as offset points, which the artifact critic correctly shows are real (they are visible in un-subtracted (d) and (e)) but which the circular-profile subtraction has merely uncovered - the surrounding dark bowtie/ring structure there is a subtraction property and was never counted. The claimed knot pair straddles the nucleus at 205 deg rather than 180 deg and at unequal brightness, with no profile-matched counter-image anywhere; the faint SW blob at r~1.3", PA~230 in (b)/(d) is diffuse, of a different surface-brightness class from the inner peaks, has no counterpart at PA~50, and lies outside the host envelope, so it is a projected patch. No thin tangential feature at fixed radius exists at any radius out to ~5" in (a)/(b); the 2.5" NW neighbour is an inclined disc, not an arc. Both alternatives are upheld and together they account for every located item, leaving nothing standing - a clumpy irregular/merging host, not a lens.

The only located evidence is the single N-S sliver ~2.6" due west of the yellow ticks, visible faintly in (a), clearly in (b) and bluish-white in (c); it lies outside the 3.5" crops, so panels (d)/(e) show only a smooth, featureless spheroid and panel (f)'s bowtie/dipole is pure circular-model artefact and carries no weight either way. The artifact critic's instrument tests (no radial spike geometry, no 60/120-deg mirrors, not on the PSF-wing line to the NNW galaxy, present in every un-subtracted panel) correctly exclude a reduction origin, so the feature is sky. The morphology critic's shell/tidal rim is overruled: the sliver's blue colour, sharp edges and internal knot are inconsistent with a same-population shell of the red host's envelope. The geometry critic's edge-on/needle reading is upheld: at 0.031"/px an arc at this radius must show measurable tangential bow and thin-for-its-radius structure, and this feature is essentially straight, of constant width, thick for r=2.6", with no counter-image on the eastern side (that quadrant is admittedly contaminated by the bright NE galaxy's halo). With the sole item accounted for by a plausible but not decisive alternative (refutation strength ~0.4) and no ring, no inner arc and no counter-image anywhere, the case is unresolved rather than clean either way, hence C; a reviewer measuring the sagitta and the eastern quadrant at full resolution would settle it.

The only located evidence is the eastern low-surface-brightness complex at r~1.6-2.3", PA~95-145, visible in the direct panels (a), (b) and as an orange/tan smudge in (c); the artifact critic offered no instrumental alternative and I make no ruling there, but both geometry and morphology independently and consistently resolve that complex as a small clumpy projected neighbour, and the pixels support them: the blob is compact (~0.5-0.7" across) with a knot chain elongated far from the local tangential direction at that position angle, it is not a thin feature at roughly constant radius, and at 0.031"/px an r~2" arc would span ~65 px from the core and would plainly show tangential curvature and surface-brightness structure, which this does not. The mirrored annulus at PA~280-320, r~1.8-2.6" in the deep panel (b) is smooth halo with no counter-arc or counter-image, and the 3.5" zooms (d)/(e) show only untextured elliptical isophotes with no inner arc or radial counter-image. Panel (f) contributes nothing either way: it shows exactly the four-lobed bowtie plus concentric rings expected when a 1-D circular profile is removed from this clearly elongated host, an artefact of the subtraction and not sky. With both items accounted for by the upheld companion-projection alternative and nothing surviving, this is a non-lens; a further tan patch at r~4.5", PA~44 at an incompatible radius reinforces that the field simply contains projected neighbours.

The catalogued galaxy at the yellow ticks is a disturbed, clumpy system whose bright body in (d)/(e) is elongated NNE-SSW; the two features the scorer cited sit at the two ends of that same major axis (r~0.9", PA~20 and r~0.75", PA~185), are compact and round with axis ratio near unity, and are bridged to the nucleus by continuous deep-stretch envelope light rather than separated from it by sky. Neither shows a trace of tangential stretch at fixed radius, and there is no arc anywhere to fit a centre of curvature to. The southern knot is unambiguously the bright NE head of the long straight needle that runs unbroken from ~0.7" south of the ticks to the SW corner of the 10" field at PA~207 - a classic edge-on disc / tidal streak whose radius grows steadily with distance, exactly the opposite of an arc at constant radius. The two strong positive lobes in (f) coincide pixel-for-pixel with these direct-image peaks and are flanked by the dark central bowtie that the circular-profile subtraction is expected to produce on an elongated deflector, so the residual adds nothing. With the merger/clumpy-host reading accounting for both items and the edge-on-disc reading independently accounting for the southern one, no item survives; this is a non-lens and no deeper data are needed to say so.

The ticked galaxy is a single smooth E-W elongated system whose light dominates the 3.5" zoom; the two located features both lie on its southern minor-axis side, at PA~188-205 (r~0.45", a hard, near-point blue dot visible in (a), (d) and (e)) and PA~172-192 (r~0.95", a soft E-W elongated orange patch in (d)/(e) that becomes the bright one-sided blob in (f)). Nothing here is tangential at a fixed radius: the two features differ in radius by a factor 2.1, in surface-brightness profile (point vs diffuse), and in hue, and the deep zoom shows only smooth, featureless halo at the mirror positions PA~350-20 at both radii, so no counter-image or counter-arc exists; item 2 subtends only ~20 deg of azimuth with no measurable curvature about the tick centre. The artifact critic correctly finds no instrumental origin - both are present in the un-subtracted panels, neither lies on the four-lobed bowtie (PA~50/140/230/320) that the circular-profile subtraction imprints on this elongated galaxy, and (b) shows no seam, stripe, snowball or bright neighbour PSF - so the (f) blob is real sky but not lensed. The geometry critic's chance/embedded-projection reading accounts for both items and is upheld; the morphology clump reading independently covers the inner blue knot. With every located item accounted for and no arc, ring or counter-image anywhere in the frame, this is a D; no deeper data is needed to settle it.

The ticked deflector is the highly flattened, E-W elongated system at the centre of the 3.5" row; everything offered as lensing evidence resolves at 0.031"/px into ordinary neighbours. Item 1, the NE 'sliver' in (a)/(b) at r~2.2", is a straight, uniformly thin needle whose long axis runs ~PA 161/341 - some 20 deg away from the local tangent to a circle about the ticks - with a compact bulge brightening at its N tip and light tapering to the SW tip: a bulge-plus-needle edge-on disk galaxy, not a tangential arc, and no sagitta is traceable over its ~1.3-1.7" length nor any counter-arc on the smooth SW envelope at PA~240. Item 2, the NW blob at r~1.15", is resolved in (d) and (e) as a round (axis ratio ~1) nucleated source with its own smooth extended halo sitting on a northward bump of the shared low-surface-brightness envelope, with no tangential elongation and no mirror image at PA~155; its radius is half that of item 1 and it lies 85 deg away in azimuth, so the pair is geometrically inconsistent with one lensed source. The artifact reviewer correctly finds both features in un-subtracted frames and offers no artefact alternative, and the bright E-W lobes plus concentric ringing about the core in (f) are the declared circular-model bowtie on an elongated host and count for nothing. With both located items absorbed by an upheld companion_projection alternative and no fixed-radius tangential structure or counter-image anywhere in (b)/(d)/(e), nothing survives.

After the rulings only the western feature survives: the knotty, roughly N-S elongated streak lying ~1.2-2.5" west (right, since E is left) of the ticked nucleus, clearly present in the un-subtracted panels (a), (b) and (c) and therefore not a subtraction product - panel (f) shows nothing but the mandated four-lobed bowtie and criss-cross inside r~1.2", which I ignore. That streak is the only item with any tangential character, and it is ambiguous: it is offset, thin (~7:1) and shows a slight concavity toward the core in (a), yet its inner end runs continuously into the bright asymmetric envelope, its long axis is tilted well away from the tangential direction at PA~271, and panel (b) is blank at the mirror azimuth (r~2", PA 74-112) where a counter-arc should sit. The northern pair (compact haloed galaxy at 2.8" PA~20, round knot at 1.5" PA~5) are round, radially inconsistent and ~90 deg off the required 180 deg pairing, so they are companions, not counter-images, and the SE plume at r~3.7" is far outside any common Einstein radius; the host itself is a smooth elliptical out to 1.7" in (d)/(e) with no arm, bar or ring. With one un-paired, partly envelope-blended streak and an otherwise interacting/tidal-looking field, the evidence neither confirms nor refutes lensing; a reviewer or deeper/multi-band data measuring the streak's curvature centre and colour against the deflector would settle whether it is an arc or a stream.

Every located item falls inside the upheld merger/close-pair reading: in the 3.5" deep and normal zooms (d)/(e) the ticked galaxy's core and the source ~1.0" NNW are both saturated, round, PSF-cored peaks of comparable brightness joined by a continuous diffuse bridge, which is a double nucleus, not a deflector plus a tangential image (geometry critic upheld for item 1 on the same pixels: no tangential axis ratio, long axis if any is radial). The proposed counter-image at r~0.9", PA~141 is a flat-topped low-surface-brightness fuzz several magnitudes below item 1's peak, so the two cannot be images of one source, and the remaining knots at 1.1" NE and 1.6" SW differ in radius by ~45% and show no tangential stretch - a clumpy tidal envelope, not a ring at fixed radius. The artifact critic's spike explanation is overruled because the rays in (b)/(f) are thin and straight while items 3 and 4 are resolved extended blobs, but that does not rescue them as lensing evidence since the merger reading already covers them. There is no thin, curved, constant-radius feature anywhere out to 5" in (a), (b) or (d), and the E-W core structure in (c)/(f) is the expected dipole/butterfly of the circular subtraction and was correctly not counted; nothing survives, hence D.

The ticked galaxy in the 3.5" deep zoom (d) is a bright, NW-SE elongated bar-like core out of whose ends two broad, low-surface-brightness sweeps emerge: the eastern one runs from just off the core at PA~20-30 out to ~1.5" by PA~150, the western/SW one mirrors it, and both remain attached to the nucleus with no gap - the hallmark of a two-armed barred/interacting disc rather than two opposed Einstein arcs, which would sit at a fixed radius and be detached from the deflector light. The 10" panels (a)-(c) confirm this: the same two sweeps close into an outer pseudo-ring at ~2-3" with the same warm colour and the same surface-brightness ladder as the host, i.e. one stellar population, not a background source. The bright opposed lobes in the subtracted panel (f) are exactly these arms plus the expected four-lobed/dipole signature of a circular profile removed from an elongated, off-centre-cored galaxy, so they add nothing independent. The compact NE knot at r~0.8", PA~56 is unresolved and bluer/whiter than the orange envelope in (e), with completely smooth envelope at the mirrored SW position - a clump or projected point source, not one image of a pair. With every located item accounted for by the arm reading (and item 3 doubly so by the projection reading), nothing survives; no deeper data is needed to settle a candidate whose arms are this plainly resolved at 0.031"/px.

The ticked galaxy is the northern member of a close, blended pair sitting in one diffuse common envelope, with the second bright nucleus only ~1.2" to the south inside the same isophotes (panels d, e, and dominating the lower half of the residual panel f). Everything the scorer located dissolves under the direct panels at NIRCam resolution: item 1 is a string of three-four discrete, essentially round compact knots on the eastern isophotal rim at r=1.30-1.42" - no tangential elongation, no continuous surface-brightness ridge, radii scattering by ~10% and a local curvature centre ~1.2" from the tick centre; item 2 is simply the eastern end of a matching four-knot chain along the northern rim at r~1.10", i.e. the same clumpy blue rim population continuing around the envelope of a tidally disturbed pair; item 3 lies squarely within the southern companion's halo and is blended light, not a counter-knot. Crucially there is no counter-image at all on the western/north-western side at r=1.0-1.6" - that envelope is smooth in both (d) and (e) - which is fatal for the broken-ring reading, and the striking vertical bowtie plus concentric ripples in (f) are the circular-profile subtraction signature and were correctly excluded by every role. What remains is a merging/interacting close pair with star-forming or tidal knots strung along its rim, so no lensing evidence survives; deeper or multi-band data would only confirm what the knots' discrete, non-tangential morphology already shows.

The only candidate features are the elongated sliver ~2.5" SW of the ticked nucleus (bottom-right of the ticks in panels a/b/c) and the faint eastward continuation of its envelope. Both critics who offered an alternative converge on companion_projection and the pixels back them: the sliver is straight over its ~1.2" length with its long axis running roughly E-W, i.e. some 35-45 deg away from the tangential direction at that azimuth, it is knotty and thick rather than a thin constant-radius band, and a second, larger curved sliver of comparable surface brightness lies farther out at r~4", PA~250-265 on the same side of the galaxy - two unrelated field objects at different radii, not a mirrored image pair. The mirror position (r~2.3-3.0", PA~30-70, NE quadrant of the deep 10" panel) shows only smooth halo, so no counter-image supports a lensing interpretation, and the 3.5" deep and colour zooms show the host to be a featureless E-W elongated envelope with no inner arc or ring. Panel (f) contributes nothing: its E-W four-lobed bowtie and central pixelated dipole are exactly the artefacts a circular azimuthally-averaged model leaves on an obviously elliptical galaxy, and the artifact critic confirmed the SW feature is present in every un-subtracted panel and shows no spike, stripe or seam signature. With both located items absorbed by an upheld projection alternative and nothing tangential surviving, this is graded D; no deeper data is needed to settle it.

The ticked galaxy in (a)/(b) is a bright bulge inside a large, mottled, disc-like envelope; the feature that drew attention - the bright ENE ridge sweeping down through E to SE - is traceable in every un-subtracted panel but its radius grows steadily with position angle (r~2.1-2.4" near PA 70-77, r~3.3-3.6" by PA 125-185), and it joins continuously onto the fainter southern plume (item 4) and is mirrored 180 degrees away by the broad SW sweep at r~3.4" (item 2). That is an arm/tidal pair winding out of the host, not a tangential arc at constant radius about the ticks, and at 0.031"/px the curvature and knotty texture are resolved well enough that the distinction is not seeing-limited. The only compact one-sided candidate, the ESE blob at r~1.1-1.3", PA~105-120 in (d), is round to within its ~0.25" extent, has a companion blob at PA~136 on the same side, and has no counterpart on the mirror side, so it reads as a projected/embedded knot; the strong cross/bowtie and concentric structure inside r<0.8" in (f) is the declared circular-profile subtraction artefact and carries no weight either way. The artifact critic offered no alternative and correctly ruled out spikes, striping and PSF wings, but with both remaining alternatives upheld every located item is accounted for and no lensing evidence survives.

Every located item is accounted for by an upheld alternative. Item 1, the only convincing off-nucleus source, is the small straight needle ~3" due south in panels (a)/(b)/(c): it has its own bright condensation, sharp ends and a straight major axis over its full 1.3" length, no curvature about the tick centre and nothing whatsoever in the mirror annulus to the north at the deep stretch - a projected companion, not one image of a lensed pair. Items 2 and 3 live at r≈0.55-0.85" inside the bright envelope, a factor ~4 smaller in radius than item 1 and therefore not part of the same source configuration; in (d)/(e) that region is only a low-contrast, boxy isophotal twist continuous with the nucleus, matching the knotty tan/orange arm-and-dust pattern visible from r≈1.5-3.5" in (c), while the S-shaped band and its knot in (f) are exactly what a 1-D azimuthally averaged model leaves on an inclined, barred/armed disc, complete with the pixel-scale checkerboard ringing around the compact core. No offset tangential feature at fixed radius survives in any direct panel, and no counter-image exists anywhere; the object reads as an inclined dusty disc galaxy with an unrelated southern neighbour.

Only two offset features were ever located and both are now explained. The ESE source (lower-left of the tick centre in (a), (b), (d), bluish-white against the orange envelope in (c)/(e)) is a compact, internally knotty object at r~1.4", PA~118 whose long axis runs roughly along the line to the nucleus rather than perpendicular to it; at 0.031"/px a lensed image of that brightness would show tangential curvature and a matching-profile counter-arc, and the annulus at r 1.2-1.7", PA 270-330 in (d)/(e) is featureless smooth halo, so it is a projected clumpy companion, not a lensed image. The western lump in (f) lies inside the concentric positive/negative ripple field that the circular profile leaves on this visibly non-circular, lumpy core (compare the bowtie plus rings straddling the centre in (f)), is round rather than tangentially extended, and has no counterpart in any un-subtracted panel; it is a subtraction residual, admissible as such precisely because it is invisible in (a)-(e). Nothing in (a)-(e) shows a fixed-radius tangential arc, a broken ring, or a pair of matched-profile images, and the host is a smooth ellipsoid with a normal envelope. With both located items accounted for by upheld alternatives, no evidence for lensing survives.

The ticked galaxy is an inclined, elongated (b/a~0.6, major axis PA~120-300) disc whose outer light is the whole story: in the 3.5" deep zoom (d) the bright NW structure (item 2) is joined to the bulge by continuous, unbroken envelope light from r~0.8" out past the panel edge and points radially at the nucleus rather than lying tangential to it, and in the 10" panels (b)/(c) that same structure sweeps round to the SW while the southern band (item 1, r~3.3" at PA~110 growing to ~4.5" at PA~230) and the fainter NE filament (item 4, r~4-5") form the counter-arm of one continuous, host-coloured, host-profiled arm/tidal system - radius growing with angle, no thin high-contrast knotty arc, no counter-arc of matching radius and brightness anywhere. Both geometry and morphology are therefore upheld over items 1, 2 and 4; the artefact critic named no alternative and correctly notes there are no spikes, seams or residual-only features (the X/bowtie in (f) is the stated circular-model artefact and the NW patch in (f) is traceable in (d)). What survives is only item 3, the compact orange knot at r~1.2", PA~138 in (e) - a single unmirrored point source sitting on the inner disc where a dust-reddened HII knot or a projected compact object is entirely expected, and with no tangential extension and no partner near PA~318 it neither confirms nor refutes lensing on its own. That single leftover keeps the case out of the D bin by the stated rule, but the evidence is strongly against a lens and no deeper data are needed to see it.

The ticked object is plainly an inclined, bar-dominated disc: in the 3.5" deep panel (d) the inner isophotes are strongly elongated ENE-WSW with a lens/bar-shaped core, and the light does not stop - it runs continuously outward into a two-armed pattern whose western arm sweeps from NNW through W to SW with monotonically growing radius (~1.2" at PA 320, ~1.5" at PA 280, >2.3" at PA 235) before merging with the diffuse 10" sheet in (b) that reaches toward the SW companion; there is no dark gap between host and 'arc', which is exactly what an Einstein arc requires and a spiral/tidal arm forbids. The SE 'knot chain' in (e) sits at PA 115-150 running radially outward at r~0.6-1.0", i.e. along the disc rather than tangentially, with no compact counterpart at the antipodal PA~309 - the classic signature of star-forming clumps on an inner arm/bar end, and the blue hue alone carries no weight here. Panel (f)'s black four-lobed bowtie and inner dipole are precisely the artefacts a circular azimuthally-averaged model leaves on an elliptical, barred host and were correctly scored as nothing. Both critics who named an alternative are upheld and the morphology reading accounts for every located item, leaving nothing standing; no deeper data is needed to settle this.

The dominant structure is not tangential about the ticked galaxy: in the deep 10" panel (b) the bright knotty lane runs continuously from just north of the ticks out past r~5" toward the NW corner, its radius growing monotonically with position angle and its width staying ~0.3" over that whole run, which is the signature of an arm/tidal lane rather than an Einstein arc thinner than its radius; in the 3.5" deep and colour zooms (d)/(e) the 'arc plus counter-image' resolves into a single string of clumps at PA~350, r~0.9-1.4" and PA~195-205, r~1.1" that is collinear with, and joined by unbroken stellar light to, the nucleus - radial, not mirrored across it - so items 3, 4 and 5 are one clump chain seen through the core, and the same features appear in the un-subtracted panels so panel (f) adds nothing independent. The faint broad band through the E/SE at r~3.5" has its centre of curvature ~2-3" WNW of the ticks and can be traced joining the main body near PA~30-50, r~4-6" in (b)/(c), i.e. an outer plume of the same disturbed host rather than a counter-arc; the artifact reviewer confirms no spike, seam, snowball or PSF wing is involved (the only point source sits at r~4.6", PA~114 with a compact round halo). With the morphological alternative accounting for every located item and nothing left at fixed radius about the deflector, this is a non-lens.

The artifact critic offered no alternative and confirmed all three items are real sky features present in the un-subtracted panels (a), (b), (d), (e) — so nothing here is a subtraction ripple; the ripples in (f) are confined to r<0.7" of the stamp centre and are the documented circular-profile artefact, which I disregard entirely. What remains is a morphology question, and at 0.031"/px the morphology is decisive: in the deep zoom (d) the NW 'blob' at r~1.1", PA~325-340 is a resolved little galaxy with a stellar nucleus at the centre of a ~1.0"x0.4" elongated envelope whose major axis runs ENE-WSW and whose isophotes curve about that nucleus, not about the yellow tick centre — an Einstein image does not carry its own point-like nucleus, and a genuine arc at this resolution would show tangential curvature and a width well under its radius. The orange band draped across the north in (e) is that companion's outer light blending into the common envelope, its surface brightness falling monotonically outward from the companion's nucleus rather than peaking at a fixed radius, and the SE 'counter-bulge' (item 3) is featureless low-SB light continuous with the host's own outer isophotes on the opposite side of the same NW-SE elongated common envelope — the classic signature of a close, interacting pair, not a matched pair of images. With both the companion-projection and merger alternatives upheld and covering all three items, and no thin tangential ridge, no counter-arc of matching surface-brightness profile, and no colour or geometric evidence that survives, nothing is left standing.

The two orange features that carried this candidate are both explained by projected/tidal structure rather than lensing: in panels (a), (b) and (c) the northern filament runs essentially straight for ~9" from the east edge over the top of the ticked galaxy to the NW corner, its distance from the ticks growing from 2.2" to >5" at both ends and its position angle fixed near 75/255 deg - no tangential curvature about the deflector, and a compact knot sits on it in the NE, so both the edge_on_disk and merger readings are supported by the pixels; the SE/S orange band in (e) is not a thin counter-arc but the illuminated inner edge of the broad orange fan that fills the SE quadrant of (c) and plumes off the south edge, its width comparable to its radius and its centre of curvature displaced ~4" from the ticks. Panel (f) contains only the declared four-lobed butterfly and inner dipole of the circular 1-D profile subtraction on an obviously elliptical bulge (PA ~135/315), which counts neither way. All that survives is item 3, a round, unresolved low-surface-brightness clump 3.8" SW in the deep panel with no tangential elongation and no counterpart - consistent with a chance projection and no support for a lens on its own; hue similarity between the two orange features is colour alone and cannot decide the case. The letter stays at C only because that unexplained clump was located, but the case is effectively a non-lens and deeper data would not change the straight-line geometry.

The 10" panels (a)/(b) show the ticked galaxy embedded in an irregular, lumpy envelope with a bright arm/plume sweeping N to NW, a fan of low-surface-brightness light beyond it to r~3.5", and a chain of tan clumps to the SW at r~2.4-3" - the classic signature of a disturbed or interacting clumpy system rather than a lens: no feature holds a fixed radius, the N/NW filament in (d) is joined to the host by a continuous stellar bridge at r~1.2" and its weak curvature implies a centre ~1.6" off the tick centre, and the annuli that would hold counter-images (r=1.5-2.1" at PA 150-190; r=2.4-3.0" at PA 25-65) are bare envelope. The one item not covered by the merger reading, the compact bump ~0.45" east of the core seen in (d) and as a one-sided bright spot on the east rim in (f), is unpaired: the western rim at the same radius is featureless, and a single asymmetric knot sitting on the edge of the saturated core with no counter-image and no tangential extent is far more naturally a clump or blended companion of this disturbed system, so the geometry refutation covers it too. The artefact reviewer found no spikes, striping, snowballs or PSF wings and every item is present in un-subtracted panels, so the circular-profile residual in (f) neither adds nor removes evidence. Nothing survives; classify as not a lens.

The ticked galaxy is a smooth E-W elongated early-type (b/a~0.6, major axis PA~100) whose deep-stretch halo in (b) and (d) is grainy at every position angle; the cited 'southern plume' at r~2.5", PA 140-240 has no azimuthal gap separating it from that halo, its boundary is concentric with the host isophotes, and its radial thickness (~1.5" at r~2.5") is over half its radius - an Einstein arc must be thinner than its radius and stand off the envelope. The blue tint on the south flank in (c)/(e) is matched by blue speckle at PA~40, ~135 and ~320 at the same radius, so it is host mottling plus two-band colour noise, not a distinctly bluer offset source, and colour alone could not carry the case in any event. The compact knot at r~1.9", PA~205 is one of several equal-brightness knots (compare PA~60, r~1.8" in d), shows no tangential elongation and has no mirrored partner at PA~25. Panel (f) shows exactly the E-W bright / N-S dark bowtie that a circular radial-profile subtraction leaves on an elliptical galaxy - an artefact of the model, not sky - and contains no offset tangential feature at constant radius traceable back into (d) or (e). Field-wide diagonal striping in (b) further depresses confidence in the faintest of the claimed structure. With every located item accounted for by the host-envelope/host-mottling alternatives and nothing surviving, this is not a lens candidate.

The only located items are (1) the compact blue-cyan blob 0.75" SSE of the ticked nucleus, obvious in the normal, deep, colour and zoom panels as a small round knot with a faint halo, and (2) a faint point-like blob ~3.6" E near the left edge of the 10" panels. Both geometry and morphology critics independently show that item 1 is round at 0.031"/px - it would span ~24 px of tangential arc if it were an image at that radius, yet shows no elongation along the local isophote - and that the envelope at the mirror position (PA~330, r~0.75") in the deep zoom (d) is featureless, so no counter-image exists where the deflector's smooth, concentric isophotes demand one. Item 2 lies at 4.8x the radius of item 1 with no curvature about the ticked galaxy, so the pair cannot be multiple images in any single-deflector configuration. The artifact critic offers no competing alternative and merely confirms both sources are real sky objects, and the bright core lobe plus wedge structure north of the core in (f) is the expected circular-profile bowtie artefact, correctly ignored by all reviewers. With the companion_projection alternative accounting for every located item and nothing tangential surviving out to ~5", this is a smooth early-type with a projected compact neighbour, not a lens; the evidence is clean enough that no further review is warranted.

The only two features located are compact and round, not tangential. In the 3.5" deep panel (d) the northern object at r~0.85", PA~350 is a clean, circular PSF-like knot with a faint plume bleeding E/NE into the host light; there is no azimuthal stretch, no curvature and the halo at the mirrored position (PA~170, r~0.85") is entirely smooth, so no counter-image exists. The bright source 3.0" SSE in (a)/(b)/(c) is a resolved compact galaxy with its own symmetric halo; its radius exceeds the northern knot's by a factor 3.5, far outside any plausible image/counter-image radius match, so the near-antipodal position angles are coincidental. Panel (b) further shows all three components sharing one N-S elongated diffuse envelope, consistent with a merging or common-envelope system rather than a deflector plus lensed images. The strong central and paired lobes in (f) are the imperfectly removed off-centre core of the 1-D circular model plus the two real sources already present in (d)/(e), and carry no independent weight. The artifact critic found no spikes, seams, snowballs or striping and offered no alternative, which leaves both items real but unlensed. With both located items accounted for by upheld companion-projection/merger explanations and no arc, curvature or matched counter-image anywhere in the field, this is not a lens; no reviewer input is needed to settle it.

The only located evidence was a thin bluish filament SW/S of the ticked galaxy (items 1-2) and a diffuse SE streamer (item 3), and both the geometry and morphology critics independently traced them, in the un-subtracted deep and colour panels, as one continuous feature: it leaves the host envelope near PA~245 at r~1.5", passes a knot at r~2.1"/PA~231, sweeps with an inflection onto the nucleus of the bright compact companion 3.2" due south, and continues past it as a low-surface-brightness plume out to r~5-6" at PA~140-165. Its radius grows monotonically with angle, its curvature changes sign, and both ends anchor on stellar nuclei - none of which a single deflector can produce - while the mirror position at r~2", PA~50 is a featureless envelope in the same deep stretch, so there is no counter-image. The artifact critic named no instrumental alternative and correctly noted that panel (f) shows only the declared circular-model bowtie plus concentric ripples, which are uninformative; that leaves no evidence for a lens and a fully self-consistent interacting-pair (bridge + tail) interpretation covering every item, hence D with no surviving items and no need for a further reviewer.

Every scored item belongs to a single continuous structure: the bright, knotted, ~1"-wide band that enters the 10" field at the SE corner label, sweeps through the yellow ticks and exits at the NW corner in panels (a), (b) and (c). In the zoom (d) that ridge is an unbroken stellar bridge across the ticked nucleus — no gap, no surface-brightness break, identical width and identical knot texture on both sides — so items 1 and 2 are the two halves of one object, not a mirrored image pair; the residual panel (f) shows only the circular-profile subtraction hole at the tick with the ridge continuing straight through it, which is a property of the 1-D subtraction and carries no weight either way. The 'second concentric strand' (item 3) is separated from the main ridge by a dark absorption lane running parallel to it over ~4", and the blue knot chain (item 4) lies ON the ridge with the reddened diffuse light on the opposite (SW) flank — the classic signature of star-forming knots plus extinction in a highly inclined, gently warped disc, exactly what the geometry and morphology critics located at r=0-5", PA 295-160. Nothing in the field is tangential at fixed radius about the ticked galaxy: the band's radius from the tick grows from 0 to beyond the 10" frame and its centre of curvature lies far off-field, so no lensing configuration about the catalogued deflector is supported and no items survive.

The ticked position lies ~1.3-1.4" SE of the dominant bright core of a large, lopsided, plume-rich late-type/disturbed system, and every located item is explained by that host. Item 1's "filament" (deep zoom, left of the E tick, PA 95-130) is not an offset, fixed-radius ridge: its surface brightness joins the envelope with no gap, and its radius opens from ~0.9" to ~1.5" as position angle grows, the signature of an outer arm/disc rim curving about the off-centre NW core, not a tangential arc about the tick centre. Item 2 is a dust-reddened knot sitting on that same rim in (c)/(e), one of at least three orange/brown knots scattered through the same galaxy at r~1.5-4", so colour adds nothing here (and colour alone could not decide it in any case). Item 3 is a round, ~0.15-0.2" compact point at PA~42 with no tangential elongation, a near-twin 1" further NE, and no counterpart at PA~220 - a projection. The artifact critic named no instrumental alternative and correctly confined the straight diffraction rays to the SE/SW corners at r>3.5", so nothing here is a detector or subtraction product; panel (f)'s central bowtie/dipole is exactly what a circular profile fit to this off-centre, non-elliptical light must leave and carries no weight either way. With no counter-image anywhere in r 0.8-1.4", PA 250-330 and both alternatives upheld over all three items, nothing survives.

Nothing lens-like survives. The ticked galaxy is a bright, moderately inclined ringed system: the deep 10" panel (b) and the colour panel (c) show several smooth, essentially closed concentric rims between ~2.3" and ~4.5" that share the host's hue, ellipticity and position angle and are centred on the ticked nucleus — the signature of resonance rings/shells, not of a thin, broken, offset tangential arc (an Einstein ring would be thinner than its radius, asymmetric in surface brightness, and would not repeat at three different radii with the host's own isophote shape). The scorer's item 3 (SSW at r~4.2") is just the major-axis segment of the outermost of those rims where it fades into the envelope, so morphology's ring_galaxy alternative covers items 2 and 3. The only high-contrast discrepant feature, the orange blob 0.85" SE at PA~115 in (d)/(e), is round and centrally peaked with its own fuzzy envelope, has an axis ratio of ~1 rather than tangential elongation about the nucleus, and has no counterpart at the mirror position PA~297 where (d) shows perfectly smooth halo light; its lobe in (f) is the same real object, not a subtraction artefact, but it is a projected/interacting companion, so geometry's companion_projection covers item 1. The artifact critic named no alternative and correctly noted that the E-W bowtie and high-frequency ripple in (f) are the expected circular-profile artefacts, which were not counted either way. With every located item accounted for by an upheld non-lens explanation, the grade is D; the configuration is unambiguous enough at NIRCam resolution that no further review is needed.

Everything offset from the ticked galaxy resolves at NIRCam sampling into a close pair, not into lensed images: panel (d) shows the northern feature as a nucleated companion (compact core at r~1.4", PA~0) embedded in a patch whose radial thickness (~0.8-1.0") is comparable to its own radius, connected to the deflector core by continuous light that makes the classic figure-eight in (b); panel (e) shows it as a distinct galaxy with its own colour/dust structure rather than a thin thread of a background source. The NE 'plume' (item 2) climbs monotonically in radius from ~1.4" at PA 10 to ~2.4" at PA 50 toward the bright galaxy 3.7" away at PA~57, which is bridge/PSF-wing geometry, not a fixed-radius arc; the large positive lobe north of the core in (f) simply reflects this real, un-subtracted companion light and cannot be counted either way. The one surviving item, the SSW envelope extension at r~1.4", PA 170-230 in (a),(b),(d),(e), is smooth, knot-free and monotonically declining outward, with no tangential thread or surface-brightness match to the northern patch, so it neither confirms nor refutes lensing but is exactly what a tidal distortion opposite a companion looks like. With no counter-image, no constant-radius curvature and no thin arc anywhere, this is best read as an interacting pair in a modest group environment; C rather than D only because that southern asymmetry was located and remains unexplained by any named alternative.

The artifact critic confirmed all three items are real sky features present in the un-subtracted panels (b), (d) and (e), so nothing here is a reduction or subtraction artefact - but reality is not lensing. The two compact knots that carry the entire case sit at r~1.0" (PA~242) and r~1.2" (PA~186) in the deep zoom (d), separated by only ~56 deg of position angle on the same southern side of the ticked core; the northern and north-eastern annulus at the same radius in (b), (d) and (e) is empty, so there is no counter-image, and neither blob is tangentially elongated - the SW object's major axis runs roughly E-W, close to the radial direction, and the S object is round with axis ratio ~1.0. Their surface-brightness profiles also differ (resolved disc-like vs compact core-plus-halo), which is inconsistent with two images of one source. Panels (a)-(c) show the whole 10" field to be a compact chain of comparably bright, similarly coloured galaxies - NE at ~2.0", S at ~2.3", SE at ~2.9" - all embedded in a common diffuse envelope, and the item-3 NE plume is continuous envelope/tidal light pointing at the NE member, not a feature at fixed radius. The residual panel (f) shows only offset positive lumps at the positions of those same companions plus the expected bowtie/ring pattern of a circular profile fit to an elliptical, blended core, which carries no weight either way. With both upheld alternatives together accounting for every located item and no tangential structure anywhere at JWST resolution, this reads as a compact group projection, letter D.

The only located evidence is the pair of compact orange knots seen in panels (c) and (e): one just inside the northern yellow tick at r~1.2", PA~0, and a larger orange blob on the western side at r~1.6-1.7", PA~297 (right-hand upper part of the zoom, since E is left). The artifact critic correctly confirmed both are real sky (they appear in the un-subtracted panels c, d, e, lie on no straight diffraction ray, and show no snowball core or striping), so nothing here is instrumental - but real is not lensed. Both critics who named an alternative converge on companion_projection and the pixels back them: the knots are round to PSF-like with axis ratio ~1 and no tangential elongation, they sit at radii differing by ~30% so they cannot lie on a common Einstein circle, they are separated by only ~62-67 deg in PA rather than straddling the nucleus, and the opposite annulus (PA 120-200 deg at r=1.1-1.8") is clean in both (d) and (e). Panels (b)/(c) show at least two further identical orange compact knots at ~2.5-3" SE and next to the NE spiral neighbour, establishing a field population of such objects; panel (d) shows only a smooth core plus a faint clumpy outer disc to r~1.2" with no arc, ring or bridge, and the only structure in (f) is the four-lobed butterfly plus concentric ringing that the circular-profile subtraction necessarily leaves on this clearly elliptical/inclined host - explicitly not evidence either way. With both located items accounted for by chance projection, nothing survives, and the grade is D; no deeper data is needed to settle this.

The two direct 10" panels show a single smooth low-surface-brightness envelope containing at least four separate nuclei - the ticked core, a compact round knot just SW of the tick centre (obvious as a distinct PSF-like nucleus in (d) and (e)), a bright diffuse elliptical ~1.5" SSW, and the elongated knotty streak ~2.7" NE that is bright already in (a) - i.e. a blended group/merger, not a deflector with images. The artifact critic's checks confirm every item survives in un-subtracted panels (so nothing here is a subtraction artefact, and the symmetric N/S lobes and concentric ripples about the tick centre in (c)/(f) are excluded by the VIEW), but survival in direct data only establishes the features are real sky, not that they are lensed. Against a lens hypothesis: item 1 is round with axis ratio ~1 at a radius where a tangential image would be visibly stretched at 0.031"/px; item 2 lies at 1.6x item 1's radius and is invisible on the normal-stretch zoom while item 1 peaks strongly there, violating surface-brightness conservation and the brighter-image-at-larger-radius expectation; item 3 has its own internal knots and a straight long axis with no counter-arc in the r=2.4-3.0", PA 210-250 annulus of (b). No feature bends concave toward the tick centre anywhere in the frame. Both critics' alternatives (companion_projection and merger) are the same physical picture and both are supported pixel-by-pixel, so all three items fall and nothing survives; letter D, scale class group by the multi-nucleus envelope rather than by any measured Einstein radius.

The artifact critic filed no alternative and correctly showed neither feature is instrumental: the northern blob at r~1.2", PA~350 appears in (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and as an offset positive blob in (f), with no straight spike or PSF wing pointing at it, and the SW extension at r~1.5", PA~220 is already present in the direct deep panels, so neither can be charged to the circular-profile subtraction - but non-instrumental is not the same as lensed. Geometry and morphology independently and consistently reduce both items to chance projection on the halo of the ticked elliptical, and the pixels back them: in the 3.5" deep panel (d) the northern source is a compact ~0.25" core wrapped in its own small round envelope, elongated radially rather than tangentially, and the mirror annulus at PA 155-200, r=1.0-1.4" is featureless in both (b) and (d); the SW clump is a diffuse low-surface-brightness patch at a different radius and a non-opposed angle, with a grossly different surface-brightness profile from the northern knot, so the two cannot be images of one source. The extra structure in (f) - the bright southern lobe and the N-S ridge - is exactly the bowtie/ring pattern a one-dimensional circular model must leave on this obviously egg-shaped, N-S elongated deflector, and carries no weight either way. Nothing curved at fixed radius survives; the bright elongated neighbour ~2.6" west and the broad envelope in (c) read as a group/merger environment, not a lens configuration. Both alternatives are upheld for every located item, no items stand, and the case is clear enough at this resolution that no further review is warranted.

Only two features were ever located, and both are accounted for by upheld non-lens alternatives. The compact source ~0.95" NNW of the ticked nucleus is round and point-like in the 3.5" deep panel (d), blue and unresolved in (e), and shows as a sharp near-PSF knot in the subtracted panel (f) with no tangential stretch at all; the mirrored position at PA~169, r~0.95" is a smooth, featureless envelope in both (d) and (b), so there is no image pair - a superposed compact companion or foreground object is the natural reading. The southern 'band' is unambiguously a resolved inclined disc galaxy at JWST resolution: in (b) and (c) it carries its own compact nucleus at the mid-point of a straight ENE-WSW ridge (PA ~73/253), the light falls symmetrically to both ends about that nucleus, and its distance from the deflector varies from ~1.6" at the WSW end to ~3.5" at the ENE end, i.e. delta_r/r ~0.8 - the opposite of a fixed-radius tangential arc, and a near-twin of the brighter inclined disc ~4" ENE. The artifact critic found no instrumental origin for either feature, but that leaves them as real sky objects, not as lensing evidence; the only structure unique to (f) is the N-S bowtie about the core, the stated artefact of the circular profile subtraction. With no curvature concentric on the ticked galaxy, no counter-image and no surface-brightness-matched partner, nothing survives, and a reviewer would add nothing here.

The ticked galaxy is unambiguously a face-on, inner-ringed multi-armed disc at JWST resolution: in the 10" deep panel (b) and the colour panel (c) the light outside the bulge is not a thin fixed-radius ring but two arms whose radius grows monotonically with azimuth (SW arm ~2.0"->3.4" over PA 195-250, NE/N arm ~2.4"->3.6" over PA 30-85), each traceable inward without a break to the bulge, dust-flecked on the E side and studded with blue star-forming knots - so item 3 is an arm and item 2 is an HII complex on the SW arm, not a lensed image. The one compact off-nuclear source, item 1 at r~0.9", PA~268, is round (axis ratio ~1, FWHM ~4-5 px in d/e), shows no tangential stretch, and has absolutely nothing at the mirror position PA~88 at the same radius in either (d) or (e); the bright one-sided point in (f) is simply that same source surviving the circular-profile subtraction, while the butterfly lobes and concentric rings around the core in (f) are the expected artefacts of the azimuthally-averaged model and were correctly not counted. The artifact critic found no instrumental explanation and named none, which is consistent: these are real sky features, just not lensing ones. With every located item accounted for by an upheld or partially upheld alternative and no tangential feature at constant radius anywhere in the direct panels, this is a non-lens; no deeper data are needed to settle it.

The only item scored was the thin bright streak ~2.6" north-northeast of the yellow tick centre, visible in the 10" normal, deep and colour panels and clipping the NE corner of the 3.5" deep zoom. The artifact critic offered no alternative and correctly ruled out spikes, cosmic rays and single-band defects (the streak appears in both bands and never depends on panel f), but the geometry and morphology critics converge on the decisive point at JWST sampling: over its ~1.5-2.3" length the feature is dead straight, with sharp parallel edges, a >5:1 axis ratio and a slight central brightening along its OWN major axis - a tangential arc at r=2.6" spanning that chord would bow toward the ticked core by ~0.24" (~10 px) and show visible curvature, and it does not. There is also no counter-image: the halo at r=2.4-2.9", PA 160-220° in the deep stretch is smooth. Panel (f) contributes nothing either way, showing exactly the four-lobed bowtie and concentric rings a circular 1-D profile leaves on this obviously elliptical, inclined galaxy, so no inner knot can be claimed. With the sole item accounted for by an upheld edge_on_disk projection and nothing left standing, this is a non-lens; no deeper data are needed to settle it.

The ticked galaxy is unambiguously a barred/inclined disc at JWST resolution: panels (a), (b) and especially the deep zoom (d) show an elongated bright bar at PA~45/225 from whose ends two diffuse, host-coloured ridges peel off with continuous light bridging them to the nucleus, their radius growing from ~0.9" to ~1.5-1.6" across the traced azimuth - the classic spiral-arm signature, far too thick (width/radius ~0.5-0.7) and radius-varying to be an Einstein arc, so items 2 and 3 fall to the morphology critic's upheld spiral_arm alternative. The only compact, colour-contrasted feature, the blue dot at r~0.6", PA~267 in (e) and as an isophote bump in (d), is round and unresolved with no tangential elongation and no counter-bump at comparable radius on the eastern side; it reads as a disc clump or projected compact companion, and the geometry critic's companion_projection stands. The artifact critic named no instrumental alternative (the 1/f striping in (b) is horizontal and orthogonal to the diagonal ridges), which does not resurrect any item. The strong one-sided positive lobe and butterfly pattern in (f) are exactly what the circular-profile subtraction produces on a barred, off-centre-cored disc and carry no weight either way. With every located item accounted for by an upheld non-lens alternative, nothing lensing-specific survives.

Both located items are accounted for by the upheld interacting-pair reading. The SE feature (visible in a, b, d, e at r~1.5", PA~146) resolves at NIRCam sampling into a compact nucleus with its own roughly circular halo, blue-cored in (e)/(c), showing no tangential elongation about the tick centre and no counter-knot on the NW side at r~1.3-1.7", PA~310-350; an arc at that radius would be a thin (width << 1.5") curved ridge, and none is present. The second item, the lopsided N/NE isophote in (b)/(d), is a smooth low-surface-brightness envelope asymmetry aligned with the host major axis (PA~55) with no ridge at constant radius and no counter-feature at PA~235 - classic interaction/isophote-twist structure inside the ~4" common diffuse envelope visible in (c). Panel (f) contributes nothing: the central black/white dipole and concentric ring there are exactly the artefacts the circular 1D profile subtraction produces on this off-centre, companion-blended, elongated core, and the artifact critic correctly found no straight spikes, striping or seam anywhere in the field. With no tangential curvature, no counter-image and no fixed-radius surface-brightness structure anywhere out to 5", nothing lens-like survives; deeper data would not change a configuration this cleanly resolved.

The ticked galaxy is a bright-cored, inclined and visibly asymmetric disc whose deep-stretch envelope (panels b and d) is lopsided to the south-west, and the two items the scorer located both dissolve under the direct panels. Item 1, the E-W streak ~2.3" south, is present in (a), (b) and (c) - so the artefact critic correctly declined an instrumental origin - but at 0.031"/px it is straight over its full ~1.2" length, ~4:1 in axis ratio, with no concavity toward the ticked core and no counter-feature in the northern annulus at the same radius; that is a projected neighbour or a detached low-surface-brightness plume, not a tangential image. Item 2, the ~1.0" southern brightening, is one of a family of similar compact knots in the disc envelope in (d) and is round rather than tangentially elongated; the strong N-S lobes around it in (f) are exactly the two-lobed bowtie a 1-D circular profile leaves on this NNW-SSE elongated core and carry no weight either way. With no curvature at fixed radius, no counter-image, and no arc-like surface-brightness structure anywhere in the 10" field, nothing survives and no lensing scale can be assigned.

The ticked object in the zoom row is a large, N-S elongated inclined/barred disc: panel (d) shows smooth elliptical isophotes out to ~1.7" broken only by one round ~0.15" knot at r~1.17", PA~120 deg with a blank mirror position at PA~300 deg, and panel (e) shows a warm NW-SE band running straight through the blue-white nucleus - a bar/dust lane at no fixed radius, i.e. item 4, the only item left standing and self-evidently host structure rather than a lensed feature. Both geometry and morphology critics are upheld on items 1-3: those clumps sit at 2.5", 2.6" and 3.8" (dr/r ~ 0.4, no common circle), at PAs 155/175/235 deg with no opposed pair, are round or diffuse with no tangential elongation in (a) or (b), and are morphologically twins of the compact galaxies scattered around the NE, E and SE edges of the 10" panels - classic companion projection on a group envelope.
